extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary critics, and cultured readers interested in wit and humour in prose
extracted.subtask_short: writing wit and humour in prose
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and guidance for producing and evaluating wit and humour (and for judging certain kinds of religious/pulpit writing) in literary prose, emphasizing distinctions between wit and humour, moral effects of rhetoric, and national/genre tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit: brevity, condensation, and analytic force
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wit is brief and sudden, and sharply defined as a crystal; it does not make pictures, it is not fantastic; but it detects an unsuspected analogy or suggests a startling or confounding inference.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit functions like reasoning raised to a higher power: concise, ingenious, and instantaneous. Examples: Johnson’s pungent analogies; many bon mots. High wit often exposes fallacy or absurdity; it requires condensation and mental ripeness. Use wit to deliver an electric intellectual shock that reveals an unexpected relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour: sympathetic presentation of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humor is the sympathetic presentation of incongruous elements in human nature and life” — representative, descriptive, and often poetic rather than analytic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour draws from situations and characteristics, is more diffuse and prolix than wit, and in its higher forms passes into poetry. It relies on sympathetic feeling and humane perception; high-culture humour should harmonize with moral sympathies. Use humour to create pictures and evoke feeling rather than to deliver terse logical hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish source and method: humour vs wit
rubrics_metrics.description: “Humour draws its materials from situations and characteristics; Wit seizes on unexpected and complex relations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing tone and technique, decide whether you aim to represent and describe (humour) or to uncover sharp analogies and paradoxes (wit). The two may overlap, but their operative mechanisms differ: empathy and depiction for humour; surprise and logical insight for wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine wit and humour where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and humour often overlap and blend; the highest minds unite both (e.g., Shakespeare, Molière).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine writing usually has wit implicit even when primarily humorous; wit tempers humour’s prolixity and prevents weariness. Aim for a balance: humour’s warmth and depiction with wit’s condensation and corrective edge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wit to check humour’s excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: “Wit is the enemy of all monotony, of all lengthiness, of all exaggeration.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour, being diffuse, risks becoming preposterous or wearisome; deploy wit to provide measure, prevent verbosity, and reintroduce tension and precision in humorous passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: High wit demands mature intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: A high order of wit is exceedingly complex and demands a ripe and strong mental development; it is rarely found in boys proportional to other powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate depth of knowledge, subtlety of analogy, and capacity for condensation. Wit that lacks musical or humane sensibility can be cold and Mephistophelian; temper intellectual cleverness with humane perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour in high culture requires moral sympathy and tact
rubrics_metrics.description: High-culture humour is allied to sympathetic emotions and demands tact; coarse or cruel humour loses place in refined taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing humour for a cultivated audience, ensure it harmonizes with moral sympathies and avoids gratuitous cruelty. Humour should ideally enlarge sympathy and not merely gloat over another’s suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coarse wit versus coarse humour: differing audience reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse and cruel humour has largely disappeared from contemporary literature, but coarse and cruel wit still provokes refined men to laugh if the shock is powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a sharp, well-crafted bon mot can overcome moral distaste by its intellectual force; by contrast, extended coarse humour is less tolerable to refined readers. Choose form accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and national tendencies affect comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: National character influences humour and wit: Voltaire exemplifies concentrated pure wit but sometimes lacks humour; German humour often lacks tact and measure and can be prolix or clumsy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying or imitating traditions, account for cultural tendencies: French cultivation of epigrammatic wit, English blend of humour and wit, German propensity for metaphysical subtilty but less comic tact. Adjust tone and pacing for readership expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermonic aim: educate souls and foster moral dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper end of the Gospel and of Christian preaching is not merely saving but educating men’s souls—creating holy dispositions, subduing egoistical pretensions, and enhancing desire that the will of God may be done on earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preaching should aim at spiritual formation and practical moral improvement rather than exciting curiosity about prophetic minutiae or apocalyptic spectacle. Avoid making listeners mere spectators of impending doom; encourage reverent contemplation of great facts and wise application of principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using prophecy as sensationalism in religious rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic interpretation that fixes the Christian mind as a spectator of gladiatorial end-times or advertises the fall of enemies is morally harmful and transports political passions onto a religious platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exploit prophecy to inflame partisan triumphalism or to create egoistic complacency. Evaluate prophetic rhetoric by its net moral effect: does it produce charity, temperance, and holiness, or hatred, fear, and preoccupation with minutiae?

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent hermeneutics and mercy over selective literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of elastic textual interpretation used to support prejudices (e.g., stretching Greek terms when convenient) while being rigidly literal when it favors harsh doctrines such as eternal misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply textual exegesis consistently and avoid twisting language to prove a preconceived moral or theological point. Favor interpretations that do not subvert compassion or reduce natural human sympathies to instruments of doctrinal triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral motivation: do not substitute reference to divine glory for direct sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions are represented as good in Dr. Cumming’s theory only if prompted by an exclusive reference to the 'glory of God'; this substitution tends to neutralize human sympathies and pervert moral development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral and literary depiction, portray benevolence and justice as strong when directly called into activity by their proper objects (suffering, need). Accessory motives (e.g., glorifying God) may aid action but should not be framed as the sole authentic motive; representing natural sympathy as morally valid is important.
